{"id": "92:13/q02", "question": "Why use al-ūlā instead of al-dunyā?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:13/q02/p1", "position": "Al-ūlā better conveys the breadth of God's ownership.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī says the Qur'an pairs al-ākhira with al-ūlā, never al-dunyā: al-ūlā includes all earlier affairs of heaven and earth, while al-dunyā concerns human worldly life. He cites 2:201, 2:86, and 4:77. Al-dunyā derives from أدنى and can mean nearer, lower, lesser, or inferior, senses ill suited to vast dominion."}]}
{"id": "92:13/q03", "question": "How does the emphatic lām in la-l-ākhira work?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:13/q03/p1", "position": "It is a non-governing lām of initiation moved into an inna clause to emphasize its delayed noun.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says the same emphatic construction appears in the adjoining declaration. Al-Itqān explains that the lām moves from initial position after inna to avoid consecutive emphatics; it can enter a subject, an inna predicate, or its delayed noun, citing لأَنْتُمْ أَشَدُّ رَهْبَةً and إِنَّ رَبِّي لَسَمِيعُ الدُّعَاءِ as well as this verse. It also notes that the lām makes an imperfect verb present in sense."}]}
{"id": "92:13/q04", "question": "Why emphasize God's ownership with the lām here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:13/q04/p1", "position": "The emphasis fits the sūra's repeated concern with wealth and possession.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts 53:25, whose context lacks the wealth theme and omits this emphatic lām."}]}
{"id": "92:13/q05", "question": "Why is the Hereafter placed before the first life?", "turns_on": "Whether the order chiefly answers deniers, expresses the afterlife's greater weight, follows this passage's context, or preserves cadence.", "positions": [{"id": "92:13/q05/p1", "position": "The deniers especially need the afterlife stressed.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the words address deniers. He rejects making rhyme the sole explanation, citing the end of al-Tawba (9:129) and noting that other wordings could also rhyme; Qur'anic ordering should not be treated as poetic meter."}, {"id": "92:13/q05/p2", "position": "The afterlife merits priority because it is better and enduring, as is its severer punishment.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites the same order in the promise to the Prophet at 93:4 and the threat concerning Pharaoh at 79:25; she explicitly rejects a mere rhyme explanation."}, {"id": "92:13/q05/p3", "position": "The order suits this passage's focus on God's ownership of both realms.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts al-Qaṣaṣ 28:70–73, where the worldly realm comes first amid worldly blessings and thanksgiving; al-Layl omits praise and puts the Hereafter first."}, {"id": "92:13/q05/p4", "position": "The fronting preserves the verse ending.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports that some interpreters give this explanation; al-Biqāʿī and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ dispute a rhyme-only account."}]}
{"id": "92:13/q06", "question": "What does it mean that both lives belong to God?", "turns_on": "Whether possession concerns the realms and everything in them, their rewards, or God's recompense within them.", "positions": [{"id": "92:13/q06/p1", "position": "God owns and governs both realms and all they contain, disposing of them as He wills.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says God gives or withholds from creatures. Muqātil is cited for dominion. Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr affirm His ownership and direction. Al-Rāzī's second interpretation says He grants both abodes as He wills. Al-Biqāʿī says He gives and withholds. Al-Ālūsī includes reward, punishment, and the fates of generous and miserly people; Study Quran reports unlimited disposal. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 5:17 for people's lack of claim beyond God's grant. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī grounds ordinary ownership in all things' dependence on God for existence and cites 13:41, 12:21, and 14:27 against any rival."}, {"id": "92:13/q06/p2", "position": "God owns the rewards of the two lives.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and al-Kalbī are cited for rewards. Abū Ḥayyān adduces Abraham's reward in this life and his righteousness in the next at 29:27. Study Quran extends the reading by implication to punishment in each. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects al-Zamakhsharī's restriction to reward because the context contains warning as well as glad tidings."}, {"id": "92:13/q06/p3", "position": "God recompenses people in both worlds.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī offers this as a further reading besides dominion and ownership of rewards."}]}
{"id": "92:13/q07", "question": "Where should people seek the good of either life?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse directs all requests to the owner or also promises worldly provision to whoever chooses the higher life.", "positions": [{"id": "92:13/q07/p1", "position": "They should seek both lives and their good from God, their sole owner.", "reasons": "A report in al-Sulamī and the explanations of al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī, and Ibn al-Jawzī say seeking either from another misses the way. Al-Rāzī says people should seek happiness in both from God. Al-Qurṭubī's Abū Ṣāliḥ report cites 4:134. Al-Qushayrī is not cited here. Qutb says there is nowhere to flee from God; al-Iṣlāḥī says neither strategy, racial standing, nor deities secure benefit and cites 53:25. He compares self-credit for wealth to Qārūn's claim at 28:78. Kuranyolu and al-Sāmarrāʾī urge seeking good and following God's guidance in both worlds."}, {"id": "92:13/q07/p2", "position": "Turning toward God for the higher life brings the lower life as well.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says one who chooses the higher necessarily receives the lower; he adduces 5:66, which describes provision from above and below."}]}
{"id": "92:13/q08", "question": "How does God's ownership bear on guidance and human responsibility?", "turns_on": "How sovereign granting and ownership relate to guidance by explanation, non-compulsion, human choice, and claims upon God.", "positions": [{"id": "92:13/q08/p1", "position": "God's dominion is unaffected by human guidance or misguidance; each person's response benefits or harms that person.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī says obedience adds nothing to God's dominion and disobedience subtracts nothing. Al-Rāzī associates this first interpretation with the Muʿtazila. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, and al-Ālūsī likewise say refusal harms the refuser and cite, in al-Ālūsī, 10:108 and 17:15. Elmalılı says no one can dispense with His guidance. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says worldly response shapes the final outcome without resolving free will; she favors the explanation attributed to al-Ṭabarī over an unnamed interpretation that raises a responsibility concern."}, {"id": "92:13/q08/p2", "position": "God guides through explanation, commands, promises, warnings, and revelation without forcing acceptance.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Rāzī reason that compulsion would undo moral responsibility or testing. Al-Iṣlāḥī says God guides through His Messenger while accepting or refusing is people's responsibility; he addresses Quraysh in verses 11–14. Al-Rāzī says this interpretation suits the Muʿtazila."}, {"id": "92:13/q08/p3", "position": "God grants guidance and the fortunes of both worlds to whom He wills.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says God grants obedience and honor here and reward later, while leaving others to disobedience, humiliation, and punishment. Al-Rāzī says people should seek happiness in both from Him and prefers this account as fitting his school over the Muʿtazilite account. Al-Bayḍāwī says He gives what He wills; al-Biqāʿī says the preceding guidance does not create an obligation upon God."}, {"id": "92:13/q08/p4", "position": "Guidance is God's favor, while people have no claim on Him beyond what He grants.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 5:17 and links this claim to the previous verse's statement of guidance. He adds that God disclosed the order of next-worldly recompense and established worldly causes and consequences."}]}
{"id": "92:13/q09", "question": "How do conduct and outcomes in both lives relate?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse foregrounds reward for guidance, both promise and threat, or the distinct ways God orders results in the two lives.", "positions": [{"id": "92:13/q09/p1", "position": "Guided people receive reward in both abodes.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī cites Abraham's descendants receiving prophecy and scripture at 29:27; al-Bayḍāwī also offers the reward of following guidance. Abū Ḥayyān cites Abraham's worldly reward and next-worldly righteousness. Al-Qāshānī says choosing the higher brings the lower as well, citing 5:66."}, {"id": "92:13/q09/p2", "position": "Both favorable and adverse outcomes depend on people's response to guidance under God's rule.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī sets obedience and honor against disobedience, humiliation, and punishment. Study Quran says a rewards reading implies punishments as well. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ stresses both glad tidings and warning and says response or refusal determines the final outcome. Al-Sāmarrāʾī notes that ease and hardship may arise in either life; givers seek the afterlife while misers seek this world."}, {"id": "92:13/q09/p3", "position": "Afterlife recompense follows God's disclosed order, and worldly results follow causes He established.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says God commands people to preserve the worldly system and guides them; neglect of its safeguards makes them deserve the consequences."}]}
{"id": "92:13/q10", "question": "How does this declaration connect with the surrounding sūra?", "turns_on": "Whether the connection is the completion of 92:12 and support for the coming outcomes, or the structural hinge between the sūra's contrasted groups.", "positions": [{"id": "92:13/q10/p1", "position": "It completes the prior statement about divine guidance and supports the ensuing warning and promise.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr connects the conjunction to 92:12 and says guidance is a favor. Al-Biqāʿī s

Corpus Coranicum says God's self-predication separates the second and third stanzas and underwrites threats and promises; Cuypers calls it the sūra's center."}, {"id": "92:13/q10/p2", "position": "It is a hinge in the sūra's paired contrasts of conduct and recompense.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum traces the saved and damned through verses 5–13 and 14–21, and reports Neuwirth's placement of verse 11 with the theological predication in verses 12–13. Al-Sāmarrāʾī reads the givers as seeking the Hereafter and misers as seeking this life, with ease or difficulty possible in either."}]}
{"id": "92:13/q11", "question": "What inward orientation do the two lives call for?", "turns_on": "Which spiritual orientation to the two lives the interpreter foregrounds.", "positions": [{"id": "92:13/q11/p1", "position": "The wise view the afterlife with certainty and the world as a lesson.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī reports this saying from an unnamed authority."}, {"id": "92:13/q11/p2", "position": "People are guided toward either the soul of spirit or the soul of nature.", "reasons": "Al-Tustarī identifies the afterlife with the first and the first life with the second."}, {"id": "92:13/q11/p3", "position": "Turning to God and choosing the higher brings both lives.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī adduces 5:66's image of provision from above and below."}]}
{"id": "92:13/q12", "question": "What did the Prophet and other prophets leave as inheritance?", "turns_on": "Whether the report names scripture, knowledge, or the disposition of any property left behind.", "positions": [{"id": "92:13/q12/p1", "position": "The Prophet left the Qur'an, described as what is between two covers.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr transmits Ibn ʿAbbās's answer and Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya's agreement, saying al-Bukhārī alone transmitted it. He explains that the Sunna clarifies the Qur'an, while God's Book is the primary inheritance, citing 35:32."}, {"id": "92:13/q12/p2", "position": "Prophets leave knowledge, and taking it yields an abundant share.", "reasons": "Abū al-Dardāʾ reports that prophets leave no dinar or dirham. Ibn Kathīr explains that they called people to the Hereafter rather than accumulating and transmitting worldly goods."}, {"id": "92:13/q12/p3", "position": "The Prophet left no inheritable property; what he left was charity.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr supports the absence of money, enslaved persons, and other property with ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith's statement. He quotes the Prophet's rule, 'We are not inherited; what we leave is charity.' Abū Bakr publicly affirmed it when asked about the inheritance; Ibn Kathīr lists ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, ʿAbbās, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, Abū Hurayra, and ʿĀʾisha among those who accepted his report."}]}
{"id": "92:13/q13", "question": "Does an occasion concerning Abū Bakr limit the passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:13/q13/p1", "position": "Some apply verses 5–19 to Abū Bakr, while their message and rulings remain general.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu reports the proposed occasion and states that general applicability does not depend on identifying a specific occasion."}]}
{"id": "92:13/q14", "question": "How are worldly and afterlife existence related?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:13/q14/p1", "position": "They are two stages of one continuous human life.", "reasons": "Asad describes human existence here and hereafter as a continuous entity."}]}
{"id": "92:15/q01", "question": "What does lā yaṣlāhā mean?", "turns_on": "Whether ṣalā names any exposure, permanent residence, or a particularly intense exposure.", "positions": [{"id": "92:15/q01/p1", "position": "To enter the Fire and feel its heat.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī glosses ṣalā as experiencing the Fire's heat; his fuller wording states that the person does not experience it. Al-Wāḥidī similarly speaks of enduring its heat."}, {"id": "92:15/q01/p2", "position": "To abide with the Fire, enduring its heat permanently.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī distinguishes the unbeliever's remaining from a sinful believer who may avoid the Fire or escape it. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says ṣaly means adhering to and remaining with it, a permanence decreed for unbelievers."}, {"id": "92:15/q01/p3", "position": "To undergo intense or enveloping exposure to fire.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says the fire surrounds the person on every side. Ibn al-Munīr reports language scholars' analogy of a sheep thrust between layers of embers: lesser exposure need not count as this ṣalā."}, {"id": "92:15/q01/p4", "position": "To warm oneself by the Fire.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports this gloss from some exegetes."}]}
{"id": "92:15/q02", "question": "How does the clause attach grammatically to the Fire just mentioned?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:15/q02/p1", "position": "It is either a second adjective of the Fire or a circumstantial clause about it.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives both parses; his fuller account links the clause to the particular Fire prepared for disbelievers. Al-Burhān observes that adjectival agreement ordinarily follows the preceding word's form, while agreement by sense is rarer."}]}
{"id": "92:15/q03", "question": "Who can undergo the Fire under the restriction 'only'?", "turns_on": "Whether the exception is literal or rhetorical, what Fire and degree of exposure it names, and whether other texts qualify it.", "positions": [{"id": "92:15/q03/p1", "position": "Only unbelievers undergo lasting residence or the full heat; sinful believers may enter and later leave.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya limits the negation to eternal burning and rejects the Murjiʾite extension to every duration. Al-Wāḥidī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Elmalılı allow temporary entry; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 2:39. Al-Alūsī distinguishes more wretched unbelievers from sinners. Al-Alūsī says this also avoids making everyone less pious enter or suffer that extreme torment."}, {"id": "92:15/q03/p2", "position": "The restriction is rhetorical: exemplary opponents are singled out as if Fire and Paradise belonged to them alone.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī answers the objection that others also burn or are saved by reading the pair as emphatic contrast. Al-Kashf praises the reading; al-Alūsī notes its Muʿtazilite premise concerning major sinners but ultimately favors it if descriptive implication is accepted. Al-Samīn reports al-Zamakhsharī's preference."}, {"id": "92:15/q03/p3", "position": "This is one particular Fire or level for deniers; other levels and punishments remain possible.", "reasons": "Abū Isḥāq al-Zajjāj distinguishes the Fire mentioned here from other ranks of Hell, including the hypocrites' lowest rank; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 2:24 as identifying a Fire prepared for unbelievers. Al-Qāḍī proposes an indefinite 'blaze' as one level; al-Rāzī counters that 70:15–16 can call all Hell a blaze. Al-Alūsī notes that the following restriction about the most pious complicates the one-level reading."}, {"id": "92:15/q03/p4", "position": "Taken literally, the restriction exempts all but unbelievers from any burning or threatened punishment.", "reasons": "The Murjiʾites infer this from the wording, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya records their denial of burning of any duration. Al-Qāḍī objects that such a reading would even exempt an unbeliever who had not denied and turned away, and would embolden sinful believers. Al-Zajjāj and al-Nasafī reject the inference; Jishumī cites consensus, license to sin and the threat against misers and sinners. Al-Alūsī observes the apparent tension with 92:17 and says sound reports must be read alongside threats to major sinners. Al-Qāḍī's objection that it invites sin is recorded in both al-Rāzī note sets."}, {"id": "92:15/q03/p5", "position": "Other punishment verses qualify the apparent general exclusion.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī gives this as another answer. His rebuttal to the charge of encouraging sin also points to present disgrace, divine anger or withholding honor and reward, and punishment in forms besides Hell. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Zajjāj cite 4:48: forgiveness of lesser sins for whomever God wills implies that some non-polytheists may be punished."}, {"id": "92:15/q03/p6", "position": "Only those fitting the stated traits approach it; all unbelievers fit denial and turning away.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim gives this as his first explanation; Jishumī prefers the first. Al-Rāzī replies to al-Qāḍī that every unbeliever denied the Prophet and turned away from examining his signs. Al-Qāḍī's objection supposes an unbeliever lacking both traits."}, {"id": "92:15/q03/p7", "position": "The most wretched is the person most entitled to Hell, without excluding others from it.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim offers this as a third explanation, and al-Qāḍī similarly treats the whole blaze as Hell while reading the exception as superior entitlement. Al-Rāzī rejects it as an unsupported departure from the apparent sense."}, {"id": "92:15/q03/p8", "position": "The Fire is named for its majority or its intended occupants, without excluding others.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim offers this as a second way to understand 'only,' alongside his other explanations; he invokes 66:6."}, {"id": "92:15/q03/p9", "position": "An ellipsis adds sinners like the most wretched to those who enter.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports the supplied wording: 'the most wretched, and whoever is like him among the sinners.'"}, {"id": "92:15/q03/p10", "position": "The address is contextual: none of the warned audience enters this Fire except those among them being addressed as deniers.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr paraphrases 'none of you enters this fire except you'; he says early Islam presented unbelievers and wholehearted pious converts as the two relevant groups, before major sins among converts complicated t

The next verse gives the converse."}, {"id": "92:15/q03/p11", "position": "Some unbelievers enter despite not having committed each specified act.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this further view concerning denial, miserliness and turning away, but says the first explanation is best."}, {"id": "92:15/q03/p12", "position": "The exception singles out the uniquely most miserable servant.", "reasons": "Qutb calls the one who undergoes it the most wretched of all servants and says no greater misery is imaginable; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects the idea of one uniquely most wretched human because eternal afterlife misery exceeds temporary worldly suffering. {"id": "92:15/q04", "question": "What does al-ashqā mean as a form?", "turns_on": "Whether afʿal has comparative force or serves as an emphatic name for the ordinary class.", "positions": [{"id": "92:15/q04/p1", "position": "The wretched person or class, with afʿal functioning without a comparison.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda and several exegetes equate al-ashqā with al-shaqī. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says Arabic can use afʿal for an emphatic active participle and cites Ṭarafa's awḥad; al-Qurṭubī's semanticists compare akbar/kabīr and ahwan/hayyin and cite 30:27. Al-Samīn invokes nonexclusive burning; al-Alūsī says this still leaves problems concerning unbelievers, poor pious people, children and the mentally ill, and cites Ṭarafa's wāḥid."}, {"id": "92:15/q04/p2", "position": "It is an elative or intensive form: the most wretched, paired with the most pious.", "reasons": "Jishumī calls ashqā and atqā elatives from shaqī and taqī. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls them intensifying degrees; al-Samīn reports al-Zamakhsharī's preference for comparative force. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the form need not identify one uniquely worst human, since permanent afterlife misery surpasses worldly suffering."}]}
{"id": "92:15/q05", "question": "Who is al-ashqā?", "turns_on": "Whether the description names a class, a divinely known person, or a reported historical individual.", "positions": [{"id": "92:15/q05/p1", "position": "The unbeliever who denies and turns away.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī identifies denial of God's signs; al-Baghawī and al-Nasafī say denial of the Messenger and departure from faith. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Wāḥidī invoke 92:16. Al-Alūsī contrasts the unbeliever with a sinful believer; Elmalılı specifies denial of guidance and truth. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the deniers knew they rejected the Messenger and Qurʾān; Iṣlāḥī says conclusive warning left rejecters no excuse."}, {"id": "92:15/q05/p2", "position": "Umayya ibn Khalaf, or Umayya and similar deniers.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to connect revelation with Umayya and peers who denied Muḥammad and earlier prophets; al-Ḍaḥḥāk's transmission names those like him. Some paired identifications allow Umayya instead of Abū Jahl; al-Itqān names Umayya alone. These reports vary over whether peers are included."}, {"id": "92:15/q05/p3", "position": "Abū Jahl.", "reasons": "Several reports give Abū Jahl as an alternative to Umayya, paired with Abū Bakr as the most pious; al-Nasafī names Abū Jahl directly."}, {"id": "92:15/q05/p4", "position": "The polytheist.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan names the polytheist; one transmission adds 'who denied and turned away' through Muʿādh rather than al-Ḥasan. Al-Wāḥidī points to 92:16, and al-Jawzī gives the same identification. Al-Qāshānī adds lack of readiness, shirk, denial of God and stubborn turning away."}, {"id": "92:15/q05/p5", "position": "Whoever God already knows to be wretched.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ gives this identification; al-Naḥḥās, al-Wāḥidī and al-Qurṭubī transmit it."}, {"id": "92:15/q05/p6", "position": "One who does neither an act of obedience nor avoidance of sin for God's sake.", "reasons": "Abū Umāma and a report from Abū Hurayra give this definition in sayings attributed to the Prophet; the latter is cited by Murjiʾites, while Sunnis read it with other punishment texts."}, {"id": "92:15/q05/p7", "position": "The owner of the palm who refused to give it up.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī associates the miser who denied reward and was eased toward Hell with the palm owner; a Medinan version has him take fallen dates from a poor family's children. The accounts differ about the buyer's payment and destination of the tree."}, {"id": "92:15/q05/p8", "position": "A Khazraji hypocrite who died persisting in hypocrisy.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī's fuller contextual account makes this identification, alongside the report of an Anṣārī palm owner and Abū al-Daḥdāḥ."}, {"id": "92:15/q05/p9", "position": "The worst among the people of Hell, while other sinners may enter.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ offers this as an alternative in al-Naḥḥās; since those worst inhabitants are unbelievers, sinful believers can still enter."}]}
{"id": "92:15/q06", "question": "What marks the denier who is called most wretched?", "turns_on": "Whether denial denotes disbelief in revelation, rejection of the Messenger, or a failure of obedience.", "positions": [{"id": "92:15/q06/p1", "position": "Denial of the Messenger and his message, and turning away from him or the Qurʾān.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this as a second reading; Abū Umāma specifies Muḥammad's message, and Ibn ʿĀshūr says the hearers knew they turned from the Messenger and Qurʾān. Ibn ʿAbbās' report adds earlier prophets."}, {"id": "92:15/q06/p2", "position": "Denial of God's signs or Book and turning from obedience.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says he does not affirm God's signs. Qatāda says he lies about God's Book and turns from God's obedience; the transmission from al-Ḥasan has Muʿādh add the next verse's phrase. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the relative clause makes actions the cause of the outcome."}, {"id": "92:15/q06/p3", "position": "Takdhīb can mean failing in obedience without an explicit verbal denial.", "reasons": "Some Arab grammarians liken it to saying fighters 'lied' by retreating; they cite an Arab expression for fighters who did not retreat and compare the Event with no falsehood in 56:2."}]}
{"id": "92:15/q07", "question": "Why single out al-ashqā against al-atqā?", "turns_on": "Whether the labels denote generic classes, intensive degrees, or hyperbolically singled-out representatives.", "positions": [{"id": "92:15/q07/p1", "position": "The two eminent opponents are portrayed as if Fire and Paradise were reserved for them.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī uses hyperbole to heighten the contrast, with Abū Jahl or Umayya opposite Abū Bakr in some identifications; al-Samīn says he retains the elative force. Al-Alūsī favors this if descriptive implication is admitted, though he notes the premise about punishment of major sinners. Al-Biqāʿī connects the emphatic distinction with unequal abodes."}, {"id": "92:15/q07/p2", "position": "They name the opposed moral classes, the wretched and the pious.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda's generic reading identifies unbelievers and believers rather than only extreme individuals; al-Samīn reports this because Fire and deliverance are not limited to extreme cases. Iṣlāḥī says the contrast is rejection versus belief, rather than degrees of wickedness or piety. Corpus Coranicum says the second moral opposition is named directly."}, {"id": "92:15/q07/p3", "position": "Their intensive forms and relative clauses make deeds the causes of opposed outcomes.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says ashqā and atqā express degree, their relative clauses point to actions causing the verdicts, and their forms make near-paronomasia or near-rhyme; Jishumī calls them elatives and says tajannub pictures the pious far from Hell on Paradise's side."}]}
{"id": "92:15/q08", "question": "What reports explain refusing Paradise or entering the Fire?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in whether they describe refusal of Paradise, flight from God, or the acts defining the Fire's entrant.", "positions": [{"id": "92:15/q08/p1", "position": "Everyone enters Paradise except the one who refuses by denial and turning away.", "reasons": "Abū Hurayra's report connects the refusal with 92:16; some versions say the Prophet recited that verse when asked who refuses. Another version defines refusal as disobedience to the Prophet and acceptance as obedience."}, {"id": "92:15/q08/p2", "position": "Only a wretched person enters the Fire: one who neither obeys God nor avoids disobedience for His sake.", "reasons": "Abū Umāma and Abū Hurayra transmit versions of this saying; al-Alūsī notes Murjiʾite use and the Sunni reading together with punishment texts concerning major sinners."}, {"id": "92:15/q08/p3", "position": "Everyone in the community enters Paradise except one who bolts or flees from God like a bad camel.", "reasons": "Abū Umāma explains that such a person denied Muḥammad's message and turned away; the reported wording varies between fleeing, rebelling and bolting, and one version explicitly attributes the simile to the Prophet."}]}

{"id": "92:15/q10", "question": "How does this warning fit the sūrah's surrounding contrasts?", "turns_on": "How the last stanza mirrors and explains the sūrah's earlier contrast.", "positions": [{"id": "92:15/q10/p1", "position": "It completes a paired account of opposed behavior and recompense.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum describes two antitheses across 5–13 and 14–21: the final stanza reverses saved/damned order, links the blessed sections by ittaqā and atqā, and places reward or warning before conduct where the earlier account places conduct first. The blaze in 14 makes the enigmatic threat in 10 concrete, comparable to disclosure in 104:4–7 and 102:3–8. Iṣlāḥī says 15–21 explains traits and reward of those cast in or shielded; al-Biqāʿī says the restriction keeps the abodes distinct."}, {"id": "92:15/q10/p2", "position": "The warning addresses persistent Quraysh deniers through prophetic revelation.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says Quraysh's persistent deniers face the blaze while those spending to attain purity are protected. Kur'an Yolu says God shows the right path and warns through revelation and prophets about Hell as the wrong path's consequence. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the contextual address as directed to the deniers themselves."}, {"id": "92:15/q10/p3", "position": "Later lines elaborate piety, selfless giving and promised satisfaction.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports Qatāda's reading that no favor is repaid, but one seeks God's face and reward; Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd apply it to Abū Bakr's freeing of Bilāl. Satisfaction may mean abundant gifts or contentment that supports obedience. Kur'an Yolu reports an Abū Bakr occasion while affirming general application."}, {"id": "92:15/q10/p4", "position": "The term al-ashqā echoes other early Makkan sūras.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum compares its use with 91:12 and 87:11, described as Group II early Makkan sūras."}]}
{"id": "92:15/q11", "question": "What reaction to the Fire warning is reported?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:15/q11/p1", "position": "ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wept and could not continue reciting it at Maghrib.", "reasons": "Mālik's account, transmitted through al-Qurṭubī by Ibn ʿĀshūr, says he switched to another sūrah."}]}
{"id": "92:15/q12", "question": "What reading observations accompany the neighboring fire warning?", "turns_on": "Different transmitted vocalizations and route practice in the nearby passage.", "positions": [{"id": "92:15/q12/p1", "position": "Abū al-Zubayr reads the preceding verb with an extra tāʾ: tatalaẓẓā.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf transmits the variant."}, {"id": "92:15/q12/p2", "position": "Some transmitted routes open non-final forms, while others read them between vowels.", "reasons": "Al-Nashr says Abū ʿAmr opens listed non-verse-final words on relevant routes, but follows his usual between-vowels reading for Mūsā where transmitted. Al-Azraq's Warsh routes through Ibn Ghalbūn and others open them; al-Taysīr and related routes read between vowels because such words are written with yāʾ, including fa-ammā man ṭaghā."}]}
{"id": "92:16/q01", "question": "What can kadhdhaba mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether takdhib is confined to explicit rejection or also names failure in conduct.", "positions": [{"id": "92:16/q01/p1", "position": "It is religious denial or rejection of the truth.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati defines ordinary kadhb as a statement at odds with reality or one's inward state, or a disappointed expectation; she says Qur'anic takdhib denotes denial of God, His signs, blessings, revelation, messengers, meeting, or the Last Day. Corpus Coranicum traces the term through early Meccan punishment legends, warnings, vice lists and judgment formulas, with possible earlier psalmic or Syriac kaddeb usage for lying, deception, treachery and religious denial; a Qur'anic coinage is therefore unnecessary."}, {"id": "92:16/q01/p2", "position": "It can mean failing to obey, without spoken denial.", "reasons": "Al-Farra and grammarians reported by al-Tabari liken it to a fighter who retreats after facing the enemy. Abu Tharwan's praise of Banu Numayr means that they fight truly and do not retreat. Al-Farra, al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi compare 56:2: the Event has no 'falsehood' because it certainly occurs. Al-Nahhas cites another Arab idiom meaning someone persisted without falling short."}]}
{"id": "92:16/q02", "question": "What did the person deny?", "turns_on": "The notes variously supply the Messenger and revelation, God's signs or Book, and truth or the divine call as the implicit object.", "positions": [{"id": "92:16/q02/p1", "position": "He denied the Messenger, his message, or the Qur'an he brought.", "reasons": "Abu Umama names what Muhammad brought; Muqatil names the Qur'an. Al-Mawardi gives denial of the Messenger as an alternative to Qatada's Book. Al-Wahidi combines the Messenger and Qur'an. Ibn Abbas's Umayya report names Muhammad and earlier prophets; al-Nasafi says the messengers. Ibn Ashur says the early audience recognized denial of the Messenger and turning from the Qur'an."}, {"id": "92:16/q02/p2", "position": "He denied God's Book or signs.", "reasons": "Qatada says God's Book. Al-Tabari says God's signs, which the person failed to affirm; al-Razi also names God's signs."}, {"id": "92:16/q02/p3", "position": "He denied truth, guidance, God, or the true call.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi and al-Alusi say truth; Qashani says God, with stubbornness and shirk; Elmalili says God's guidance; Qutb says the call and promised guidance; Tabatabai says the true call. Bint al-Shati describes the denier without a narrower object."}]}
{"id": "92:16/q03", "question": "What does tawallā mean here, and from what does he turn?", "turns_on": "The implicit object is variously faith or revelation, obedience, and truth or its proofs.", "positions": [{"id": "92:16/q03/p1", "position": "He turns away from faith, the Messenger, or the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Abu Umama says he turns away from Muhammad; Muqatil, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi say faith. Ibn Ashur says the Qur'an. Bint al-Shati gives the literal sense of turning away or retreating and cites parallel pairings with disbelief or denial at 88:22-23, 75:31-32, 20:48 and 70:15-16."}, {"id": "92:16/q03/p2", "position": "He turns away from obedience or practical action.", "reasons": "Qatada specifies obedience to God, al-Mawardi alternatively obedience to the Messenger. Al-Baydawi and al-Alusi likewise say obedience. Al-Razi says obedience and Ibn Kathir explains refusal to act with one's limbs. Al-Biqai adds refusal to give wealth for self-purification."}, {"id": "92:16/q03/p3", "position": "He turns away from truth, guidance, or examining the proofs.", "reasons": "Al-Biqai calls this arrogant and stubborn rejection of truth; Elmalili and Qutb emphasize guidance; Tabatabai calls it turning from the true call. Al-Razi argues that every unbeliever turns away from examining the prophet's proofs, so all fit the wording."}]}
{"id": "92:16/q04", "question": "Who is the person described by 'the one who denied and turned away'?", "turns_on": "Whether the relative description marks a general class, disobedient refusers, or particular Meccan opponents.", "positions": [{"id": "92:16/q04/p1", "position": "The description identifies an unbeliever or polytheist as the wretched person.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan identifies the most wretched as a polytheist, while Mu'adh adds the phrase 'who denied and turned away.' Ibn Atiyya says the denial marks the preceding ashqa as an unbeliever. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi, al-Biqai, Elmalili, Ibn Ashur and Tabatabai read the category as unbelievers. Tabatabai says it is any unbeliever answering the true call this way, rather than one individual; Elmalili distinguishes a sinner who turns away without denial."}, {"id": "92:16/q04/p2", "position": "It includes whoever refuses God or the Messenger through disobedience.", "reasons": "Abu Hurayra's and Abu Umama's reports explain the person as a refuser of Paradise, one who flees God. Prophetic reports define refusal as disobedience and the wretch as one who neither obeys God nor abstains from sin for Him. Al-Farra's figurative sense allows practical failure to count as denial."}, {"id": "92:16/q04/p3", "position": "The wretched one was Umayya ibn Khalaf and others like him.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas says the passage was revealed about Umayya and others who denied Muhammad and earlier prophets; the report through al-Dahhak likewise names Umayya and those like him. Al-Zamakhshari offers Abu Jahl or Umayya as the eminent unbeliever balanced against Abu Bakr."}, {"id": "92:16/q04/p4", "position": "It identifies whoever was wretched in God's prior knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Farra is reported by al-Qurtubi as locating the person's wretchedness in God's knowledge."}]}
{"id": "92:16/q05", "question": "How do denial and turning away work together?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:16/q05/p1", "position": "Denial is inward rejection, and turning away is failure in outward action.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir assigns denial to the heart and refusal of action to the limbs. Al-Biqai assigns denial to the knowing faculty and arrogant turning away to the acting faculty, including refusal to give purifying wealth. Corpus Coranicum notes the established pairing in 96:13, 79:21-22 and 75:32; 88:23 pairs turning away with kafara instead."}]}

 the relative clauses for the wretched and pious point to the actions causing their respective fates."}, {"id": "92:16/q06/p2", "position": "The preceding exclusion clause can be another descriptor or a circumstantial clause.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says this clause concerns the particular Fire prepared for disbelievers, comparing 2:24, and that 92:17 confirms it."}]}
{"id": "92:16/q07", "question": "What force does 'the most wretched' have in identifying this person?", "turns_on": "Whether af'al is noncomparative, emphatically superlative, or a class description grounded in eternal misery.", "positions": [{"id": "92:16/q07/p1", "position": "Ashqa means 'wretched' without comparative force.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda and Ibn Atiyya cite Tarafa's awhad for Arabic af'al used as fa'il. Ibn al-Jawzi gives the same proof; al-Razi compares 'not the one-and-only.' Al-Samin says this reading allows the Fire and its avoidance to include less extreme cases. Al-Burhan notes that adjectives normally agree in form with their antecedents, while agreement by meaning is rarer."}, {"id": "92:16/q07/p2", "position": "It retains a superlative or comparative force for an eminent unbeliever.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari balances an eminent unbeliever, Abu Jahl or Umayya, against Abu Bakr and calls the exclusive wording hyperbole as though Fire and Paradise were created for the two. Bint al-Shati calls the definite unqualified ashqa absolutely most wretched. She distinguishes the Thamud construct ashqaha, limited to their own most wretched member, and compares definite ashqa in al-A'la and al-Layl; she traces shaqa' as hardship, then Qur'anic misguidance and disobedience through 20:123, 23:106, 11:105-106, 20:117 and Maryam. Al-Raghib says misery entails toil but not all toil is misery. Islahi says rejected messengers after conclusive warning have no excuse, so are the most wretched."}, {"id": "92:16/q07/p3", "position": "It names any unbeliever, since eternal misery outweighs temporary worldly suffering.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says ashqa does not single out the most wretched human being; the relative description marks any unbeliever who denies the true call and turns away."}]}
{"id": "92:16/q08", "question": "Whom does the Fire's restriction include or exclude?", "turns_on": "Whether the exclusion is absolute, limited to a particular Fire or duration, figurative, or supplied with omitted entrants; whether the traits cover all unbelievers.", "positions": [{"id": "92:16/q08/p1", "position": "Only unbelievers enter Hell or are threatened with its punishment.", "reasons": "The Murji'ites infer exclusivity from the warning's restriction to the denier. Al-Qadi points out that a literal restriction would even exclude an unbeliever who had not denied and turned away, and says it appears to assure sinful believers that their sin cannot harm them. Jishumi and al-Zajjaj reject the exclusionary inference."}, {"id": "92:16/q08/p2", "position": "The verse concerns one particular Fire or level, so other sinners may face punishment.", "reasons": "Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj says Hell has ranks; al-Qurtubi mentions the hypocrites' lowest level and other threatened punishments. Al-Wahidi likewise distinguishes levels. Ibn Ashur compares the specific Fire prepared for unbelievers at 2:24 and points to 92:17. Al-Zajjaj and al-Qurtubi cite 4:48: discretionary forgiveness of sins short of shirk would be idle if all such sinners were exempt."}, {"id": "92:16/q08/p3", "position": "The exclusion is about permanent burning; sinful believers may enter but do not remain.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi says sinful non-polytheists are omitted in abbreviated wording and yusliha denotes enduring heat, not necessarily eternity; abiding applies to the denying polytheist. Al-Nasafi and al-Biqai explicitly limit eternal exposure to the unbeliever. Elmalili says a sinner who turns away without denial may enter but does not remain."}, {"id": "92:16/q08/p4", "position": "The stated traits identify those who approach the Fire, without excluding other sinners.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim's first explanation of 'none enters it but the most wretched' is that the stated traits mark its intended subject. Jishumi prefers this first explanation and objects that absolute exclusion contradicts consensus, invites sin and conflicts with threats to the miser and sinner. Al-Razi counters that blame, divine anger and loss of honor deter sin, and God can punish otherwise."}, {"id": "92:16/q08/p5", "position": "The Fire is named for the majority or its intended occupants.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim offers this as a way to read the restriction without excluding every other entrant."}, {"id": "92:16/q08/p6", "position": "The wording names those most deserving of the Fire.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim offers this alternative; al-Razi rejects reducing ashqa to 'more deserving' because it abandons the apparent meaning without evidence."}, {"id": "92:16/q08/p7", "position": "An ellipsis includes the most wretched and sinners like him.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports the supplied phrase 'and whoever is like him among the sinners.' Al-Wahidi also reports an abbreviated mention of sinful non-polytheists, adding that entry need not mean eternal abode."}, {"id": "92:16/q08/p8", "position": "Not every unbeliever must have performed each listed act.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports a view that some unbelievers enter without each specified denial, miserliness and turning away; he prefers Abu Muslim's first explanation."}, {"id": "92:16/q08/p9", "position": "All unbelievers do fit the paired description.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says every unbeliever denies the prophet's claim and turns from examining its proofs; this answers al-Qadi's hypothetical unbeliever without those traits."}, {"id": "92:16/q08/p10", "position": "The apparent restriction could encourage or virtually permit sin.", "reasons": "Al-Qadi says a sinful believer might infer that sin cannot harm one who neither denied nor turned away. Jishumi raises the same concern. Al-Razi rejects it: present disgrace, divine anger, withheld honor and reward, and other forms of punishment still deter."}]}
{"id": "92:16/q09", "question": "What do the transmitted sayings say about the denier's fate?", "turns_on": "The reports give complementary formulations of refusal of Paradise and qualification for the Fire.", "positions": [{"id": "92:16/q09/p1", "position": "Everyone enters Paradise except one who refuses; the denier who turns away is the refuser.", "reasons": "Abu Hurayra's report identifies the refuser by reciting this description. Versions through Makhul and Abu Umama say the community enters Paradise except one who flees God like a bad camel from its owner; one calls it the gentlest saying heard. Prophetic versions explain that obedience to the Prophet leads to Paradise and disobedience is refusal."}, {"id": "92:16/q09/p2", "position": "Only a wretch enters Hell: one who neither obeys God nor leaves a sin for His sake.", "reasons": "The Prophet's definition is transmitted through Abu Hurayra and Abu Umama in the cited collections; the report shifts attention from a named person to conduct."}]}
{"id": "92:16/q10", "question": "What occasion or incident is connected to this warning?", "turns_on": "Whether the reports specify the original occasion or serve as applications of a general early Meccan warning.", "positions": [{"id": "92:16/q10/p1", "position": "The passage concerns Umayya ibn Khalaf and others who denied Muhammad.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas names Umayya and others who denied Muhammad and earlier prophets; the al-Dahhak route adds those like him. Al-Zamakhshari also offers Abu Jahl or Umayya as the outstanding unbeliever in a balanced contrast."}, {"id": "92:16/q10/p2", "position": "The refusal can be mapped to a Medinan palm owner who mistreated poor children.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports that a palm owner snatched fallen dates from the children and rejected the Prophet's offer of a Paradise palm; another man bought the tree for forty palms and donated it. {"id": "92:16/q11", "question": "Why pair this description with the opposite figure in the sūra?", "turns_on": "The notes explain the contrast both through omitted opposing acts and through the sūra's repeated, reversed arrangement.", "positions": [{"id": "92:16/q11/p1", "position": "The opposed conduct of denier and giver makes their opposite outcomes intelligible.", "reasons": "Al-Biqai says reciprocal omission lets denial imply its opposite in the pious person and later giving imply its omitted opposite for the wretched. Ibn Ashur says the relative clauses make each action the cause of its outcome. Islahi calls it a contrast of messenger rejecters and believers rather than grades of virtue."}, {"id": "92:16/q11/p2", "position": "The closing stanza reverses and mirrors the earlier antitheses.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum says the sūra first contrasts conduct and recompense in verses 5-13, then again in 14-21; the final stanza reverses the earlier saved/damned order, links ittaqa at 92:5 to atqa at 92:17, and presents warning or promise before the conduct rather than after it. It says 92:14 reveals the blazing Fire implicit in 92:10, comparable to 104:4-7 and 102:3-8.

{"id": "92:16/q12", "question": "How is the warning directed and received?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:16/q12/p1", "position": "It warns the rejecters of guidance, especially Quraysh, of a blazing Fire.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawi calls it a warning to Mecca. Islahi addresses persistent Quraysh deniers, setting them against those who spend to purify themselves; Kur'an Yolu says God guides through revelation and prophets and warns against Hell as the consequence of the wrong path."}, {"id": "92:16/q12/p2", "position": "The warning moved Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz to tears in prayer.", "reasons": "Malik recounts that during Maghrib Umar cried so hard at the blazing Fire warning that he could not continue this sūra and recited another."}]}
{"id": "92:16/q13", "question": "What does the surrounding language say about burning and being spared?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:16/q13/p1", "position": "Salaa means roasting or punishment in blazing fire.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati distinguishes it from warmth sought for comfort."}, {"id": "92:16/q13/p2", "position": "The most pious is spared the Fire by God before reaching its harm.", "reasons": "Al-Samarrai says the passive verb attributes rescue to God, creator of people and Fire, rather than human power, even for the most pious giver; he cites 3:185 and 19:71-72. {"id": "92:17/q01", "question": "What does being kept from it entail?", "turns_on": "Whether the promise describes complete distance from Hell or a contrast with the severe torment others can suffer.", "positions": [{"id": "92:17/q01/p1", "position": "God sets the God-fearing person far from the Fire, so he does not enter it.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi, al-Jishumi, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, and al-Alusi explain the verb as distancing or putting to one side; al-Jishumi pictures him on Paradise's side. Al-Baydawi and al-Biqa'i specify that full avoidance of idolatry and sins prevents entry; Elmalılı adds an easy passage to Paradise. Al-Tabari calls it protection from the blazing Fire."}, {"id": "92:17/q01/p2", "position": "Lesser believers may enter Hell yet be spared its most severe burning or leave after punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi distinguishes entry from burning for one avoiding shirk but committing sins. Al-Biqa'i says such a sinner may enter and later leave. Ibn al-Munir, quoted by al-Alusi, describes ṣaly as roasting between layers of embers; this allows lesser punishments. Al-Alusi says the most pious do not enter."}]}
{"id": "92:17/q02", "question": "How is yujannabuhā constructed?", "turns_on": "Whether the object is explicit and how the passive promotes the person protected.", "positions": [{"id": "92:17/q02/p1", "position": "Jannaba takes two objects; in the passive al-atqā becomes the subject and the Fire pronoun remains its other object.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi derives the verb from putting a person's side away and notes its common distancing sense; his two summaries give differing object numbering while agreeing on the passive construction."}, {"id": "92:17/q02/p2", "position": "When an object is unexpressed, jannaba can mean keeping someone from good.", "reasons": "Al-Raghib, quoted by al-Alusi, connects this usage with putting a person's side away; the explicit Fire pronoun here specifies the object."}]}
{"id": "92:17/q03", "question": "What does the future passive wording suggest?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:17/q03/p1", "position": "The future particle promises certainty after a respite, and the passive portrays separation from Hell as effortless.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i draws both effects from the future particle and passive form."}]}
{"id": "92:17/q04", "question": "What degree of piety does al-atqā express?", "turns_on": "Whether the afʿal form is an ordinary descriptor, an absolute rank, or a comparison within a stated group.", "positions": [{"id": "92:17/q04/p1", "position": "The form can mean simply a pious person, naming the pious class.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari and al-Tabrisi cite Tarafa's awḥad for wāḥid; al-Qurtubi adds akbar for kabīr and ahwan for hayyin, mentioning 30:27. Al-Alusi repeats the poetic evidence but says generic elatives alone do not settle the restriction difficulty.
